title: vLLM x Mooncake Store: distributed KV-cache pool with GPUDirect RDMA delivers 3.8x throughput and 46x lower TTFT on agentic traces
event_hint: Official vLLM engineering blog integrating Mooncake's distributed KV-cache store into vLLM, achieving large agentic-workload speedups with SM-free zero-copy RDMA transfer and linear scaling to 60 GPUs
problem: Agentic LLM workloads (e.g., Claude Code, OpenClaw, Codex) are long-horizon and multi-turn: by turn 30 context reaches ~80K tokens (longest >180K), yet each turn adds only a few hundred to a few thousand new tokens — the rest is reusable prefix. Local KV-cache offloading to CPU DRAM/disk is limited by (a) capacity/eviction under many long sessions (a 100K-token context is ~3.8 GB for Kimi-2.5 FP8) and (b) cross-instance misses when a router migrates a session to an instance that has never seen the prefix, forcing full recomputation.
mechanism: A distributed KV-cache pool is built with Mooncake Store. A master server manages cluster-wide metadata (KV block hashes, sizes), service discovery, and dead-node cleanup; Mooncake clients run on GPU nodes managing local CPU/DRAM/SSD and interconnect via RDMA. vLLM integration uses the existing KVconnector interface: (1) scheduler-side — on a new request, vLLM hashes the prompt's token blocks, queries the master for matching KV blocks, and uses results to guide scheduling; (2) worker-side — each GPU worker embeds a Mooncake client, registers GPU KV-cache memory as RDMA buffers, and uses GPUDirect RDMA to read/write KV blocks directly between GPU HBM and CPU memory with NO staging buffer and NO SM consumption. All RDMA descriptor preparation and issuance runs on a dedicated background I/O thread, keeping the transfer fully asynchronous and off the main CPU path. A MultiConnector wrapper chains PD-disaggregation and store connectors so prefill instances store and recover prefix KV blocks from the pool while decode instances receive them via the PD connector.

evidence.claim: On realistic Codex agentic traces (1P1D, 12 GPUs), the distributed KV-cache pool improved vLLM throughput 3.8x, reduced P50 TTFT 46x, and reduced end-to-end latency 8.6x.
evidence.source_locator: Performance section / TL;DR: "3.8x higher throughput, 46x lower TTFT, and 8.6x lower end-to-end latency on realistic agentic traces"
evidence.condition: Codex agentic traces, Kimi-2.5 NVFP4 on GB200, 1P1D, 12 GPUs

evidence.claim: Cache hit rate rose from 1.7% (only system prompt cached) to 92.2% (nearly entire prefix cached) with the distributed pool.
evidence.source_locator: Performance section: "from 1.7%, where only the system prompt is cached, to 92.2%, where nearly the entire prefix is cached"

evidence.claim: KV blocks are moved directly between GPU HBM and CPU memory via GPUDirect RDMA, requiring no staging buffer and consuming no SMs, with multi-NIC pooling and topology-aware path selection.
evidence.source_locator: Design highlights, SM-free section: "using the RDMA NIC and GPUDirect RDMA to move KV blocks directly between GPU HBM and CPU memory. This path requires no staging buffer and does not consume SMs"

evidence.claim: Under round-robin routing designed to stress cross-node traffic, vLLM with Mooncake Store maintained >95% cache hit rate and scaled nearly linearly to 60 GPUs.
evidence.source_locator: Scaling section: "vLLM consistently achieves a cache hit rate above 95%, and the system scales nearly linearly to 60 GPUs"
evidence.value: >95% hit rate; near-linear scaling to 60 GPUs
evidence.baseline: would cause massive cache misses without distributed pool
evidence.condition: synthetic Codex-derived workload, round-robin routing, sessions scaled 75→375 with GPUs

evidence.claim: Codex/SWE-bench Pro agentic traces show 94.2% cache hit rate, 131:1 input-to-output ratio, and median context growth from 12K to 80K tokens over a trace (610 traces, median 33 turns).
evidence.source_locator: Agentic workloads section: "94.2% cache hit rate"; "131:1 input-to-output ratio"; "Median context growth from 12K to 80K tokens per trace"

evaluation_context: Engineering benchmark blog from the vLLM team. Hardware: NVIDIA GB200 nodes; Kimi-2.5 NVFP4 model; prefill TP4, decode DP8+EP for best latency-throughput tradeoff; realistic-trace test used 1P1D with 12 GPUs; scalability test used 20K common + 10K first-input tokens, 2048 tokens/turn input, 900 output tokens, 30 turns, sessions scaled 75→375 across growing GPU counts up to 60. Round-robin routing was deliberately used to force cross-node KV fetches. Dataset (Codex/SWE-bench Pro traces) open-sourced. Agentic traces also collected from GPT-5.4.
limitations: Benchmark numbers are vendor-reported (vLLM team) on their own integration; no third-party reproduction is referenced. [explicit] Scalability test used a synthetic dataset derived from Codex (controlled), not the raw agentic traces — real-trace results at 60-GPU scale are not reported. [explicit] Decode instances do not currently read prefix KV from the pool directly; prefill loads and forwards via the PD connector — the authors flag multi-path loading as future work, so decode-side datapath is not yet optimized. [explicit] Roadmap items (distributed disk offloading to NVMe, hybrid-model caching, cache-aware routing, multi-node NVLink/DualPath) are stated as 'what's next' and not yet implemented. [explicit] No network-bandwidth utilization, RDMA-throughput, or P95/P99 network-latency figures are reported — the evaluation is throughput/TTFT/E2E-latency centric. [explicit]
project_relevance: Directly and strongly relevant to the KVCache cross-node transfer and TPN/inference-network briefing interests. This is a concrete, measured realization of cross-instance KV-cache sharing via RDMA — the core mechanism TPN-style networks must carry. The GPUDirect-RDMA zero-copy, SM-free transfer path and multi-NIC pooling directly inform how a state-aware inference network should expose KV-transfer bandwidth. The agentic-trace characterization (131:1 in:out ratio, 94% prefix reuse, 80K+ contexts) quantifies why distributed KV pools matter for Agent-acceleration workloads. The 1.7%→92.2% hit-rate jump and near-linear scaling to 60 GPUs are the kind of end-to-end evidence the briefing values. Gap: no network-layer utilization/latency-percentile data, so the 'network-aware' angle is implicit (RDMA fabric) rather than explicitly TPN-branded.
source_notes: Official vLLM blog; primary engineering source with open-sourced trace dataset and benchmark artifact repositories linked.

Implementation builds on Mooncake (the KVCache-centric architecture in arXiv:2407.00079) and was partly inspired by vLLM-Ascend; initial implementation by Chao Lei (Ant Group), agentic trace analysis by Zijing Liu (Inferact).
